The timing (onset during gym exercise), absence of systemic symptoms (no fever, weight loss, bowel/bladder dysfunction), and normal neurological exam (intact sensation, motor strength, and reflexes) argue against serious non-mechanical causes such as infection, malignancy, or cauda equina syndrome. Physical exam reveals localized lumbar tenderness, limited range of motion, and a positive straight leg raise test—highly suggestive of nerve root irritation. Crucially, MRI confirms an L5–S1 disc herniation with nerve root impingement, which anatomically explains the radicular pattern (L5 or S1 root involvement can cause lateral leg/foot pain; given radiation to the foot and positive SLR, S1 is likely involved, though precise dermatomal mapping would refine this). Her age, lack of comorbidities, and mechanical onset further support a primary lumbar disc herniation as the underlying etiology—not degenerative stenosis, spondylolisthesis, or inflammatory arthropathy.

DIAGNOSIS: Lumbar disc herniation at L5–S1 with associated radiculopathy
